You can dynamically generate an /etc/modprobe.conf file that corresponds to all your currently installed modules by running modprobe -c. This command generates a line file that looks like this:

```
#This file was generated by modprobe -c
path[pcmcmia]=lib/modules/preferred
path[pcmcmia]=lib/modules/default
path[pcmcmia]=lib/modules/2.6.6
path[misc]=lib/modules/2.6.6
...

# Aliases
alias block-major-1 rd
alias block-major-2 floppy
...
nalias char-major-4 serial
alias char-major-5 serial
alias char-major-6 lp
...
alias dos msdos
alias plip0 plip
alias ppp0 ppp
options ie=0x0340 irq=9
```

The path statements tell where a particular module can be found. You can modify or add entries of this type if you want to keep your modules in a nonstandard location.

The alias statement maps between block major device numbers, character device numbers, filesystems, network devices, and network protocols and the corresponding module names.

The options are not dynamically generated but must be manually added by an administrator. They specify options that should be passed to a module when it is loaded. For example, we could use the following line to tell the snarf module its proper I/O address and interrupt vector:

```
options snarf io=0xXXX irq-X
```

modprobe also understands install and remove. These statements allow commands to be executed when a specific module is inserted into or removed from the running kernel.

# Loadable kernel modules in Solaris

In Solaris, virtually everything is a loadable module. The modinfo command lists the modules that are currently loaded.

> 3. If you are using really old PC hardware, it can be a challenge to create a configuration in which device interrupt vectors (IRQs) and I/O ports do not overlap. You can view the current assignment on your system by examining the contents of /proc/interrupts and /proc/ioports, respectively. The overlap isn't typically an issue with current mainstream PC hardware.
